title: Do private businesses in Japan have to provide reasonable accommodation for people with disabilities?
description: Since April 1, 2024, businesses in Japan must provide reasonable accommodation to people with disabilities: Article 8, the Basic Policy and staff training.
shortAnswer: Yes. Since April 1, 2024, Article 8(2) of Japan's Act for Eliminating Discrimination against Persons with Disabilities makes reasonable accommodation a legal duty for every private business, not just an effort duty. When a person with a disability asks for a barrier to be removed and the burden is not excessive, the business must respond. Article 5 asks businesses to train relevant staff, and the 2023 Basic Policy treats staff training as part of preparing the environment.
keyTakeaways: The amending Act No. 56 of 2021 took effect on April 1, 2024 and changed reasonable accommodation by private businesses from an effort duty to a legal duty.
"Business operator" covers any person that carries on business repeatedly, for profit or not, including sole proprietors, social welfare corporations and nonprofit organizations.
The Cabinet's Basic Policy of March 14, 2023 lists five factors for judging excessive burden and requires businesses to explain their reasons when they decline.
Article 5 sets an effort duty to train relevant staff, and the Basic Policy says environmental improvement includes staff training and internal rules, not only physical accessibility.
Accommodation for a business's own employees falls under the Act on Promotion of Employment of Persons with Disabilities, not this Act (Article 13).
regulator: Cabinet Office (overall policy) and the competent ministers for each business sector, who issue sector guidelines under Article 11
appliesTo: All private business operators that deal with customers, users or the public, including sole proprietors and nonprofit organizations
Customer facing staff in retail, hospitality, transport, finance, healthcare, education and online services
Managers who decide whether a requested accommodation is an excessive burden
Staff who run consultation or complaint desks
Exam, certification and training providers that run assessments

sections.heading: What changed for private businesses on April 1, 2024?

blocks.text: On April 1, 2024, reasonable accommodation became a legal obligation for private businesses in Japan. The Cabinet Office confirms on its [disability discrimination policy page](https://www8.cao.go.jp/shougai/suishin/sabekai.html) that the Act was amended in May 2021 (Act No. 56 of 2021) and that the amendment took effect on April 1, 2024; the date was fixed by Cabinet Order No. 60 of 2023.

The Act for Eliminating Discrimination against Persons with Disabilities (Shōgai o Riyū to Suru Sabetsu no Kaishō no Suishin ni Kansuru Hōritsu, Act No. 65 of 2013) first took effect on April 1, 2016. From then, government bodies were already legally bound to provide reasonable accommodation, while private businesses only had to make efforts. As at November 2026, the [current text of Article 8 on e-Gov](https://laws.e-gov.go.jp/law/425AC0000000065) places both duties on businesses in identical terms to those that apply to government bodies under Article 7.

The Cabinet adopted a revised Basic Policy on March 14, 2023, which applies from the amendment's commencement date. It records that "the 2021 amendment changed the provision of reasonable accommodation by businesses into a legal obligation" (translated) and asks the competent ministers to revise their sector guidelines accordingly.

sections.heading: What does Article 8 require of businesses?

blocks.text: Article 8 contains two duties. Article 8(1) prohibits unjust discriminatory treatment on the ground of disability. Article 8(2) requires reasonable accommodation when a person with a disability expresses that they currently need a social barrier removed and the burden of doing so is not excessive.

Under Article 8(2) the accommodation must be necessary and reasonable and must take account of the person's sex, age and the state of their disability. Article 2 defines a social barrier broadly: anything in society, including things, systems, practices and ideas, that makes daily or social life difficult for a person with a disability. That definition reflects the social model of disability, which the Basic Policy asks every sector to promote.

The Basic Policy gives examples of conduct that may breach Article 8(1). One is uniformly lowering the quality of service, such as language or attitude, because a customer has a disability. Another is refusing a request to use a digital device in an exam, without considering adjustments, simply because there is no precedent.

sections.heading: Who counts as a business operator under the Act?

blocks.text: A business operator is anyone that carries on commercial or other business, other than national and local government bodies and certain public corporations. Article 2(vii) sets the definition, and the Basic Policy explains that it applies regardless of whether the activity is for profit and whether the operator is an individual or a company.

According to the Basic Policy, the test is whether a person intends to carry out the same kind of act repeatedly. Sole proprietors, people who run unpaid activities, and nonprofit social welfare corporations and specified nonprofit corporations are all covered. Online businesses are not excluded, so a digital service that receives an accessibility request is in scope in the same way as a shop counter.

sections.heading: How do businesses decide whether a burden is excessive?

blocks.text: Businesses must judge excessive burden case by case, considering the specific situation comprehensively and objectively. The Basic Policy lists five factors and expects the business to explain its reasons politely if it decides that a request would be an excessive burden.

blocks.text: The Basic Policy stresses constructive dialogue (kensetsuteki taiwa). Both sides should share what the person already does to work around barriers and what the business can offer, and alternatives should be considered. Its retail example: if a store cannot accompany a visually impaired customer around the shop at a busy time, staff can offer to take the shopping list and gather the items instead.

sections.heading: Does the Act require staff training?

blocks.text: The Act sets an effort duty, not a strict duty, to train staff. Article 5 says government bodies and businesses must endeavor to improve facilities, equipment, "training for relevant staff" and other necessary parts of the environment so that reasonable accommodation can be provided properly.

The [2023 Basic Policy](https://www8.cao.go.jp/shougai/suishin/sabekai/kihonhoushin/r05/txt/honbun.txt) builds on this in three ways. First, it states that environmental improvement covers soft measures such as staff training and internal rules, not only barrier free facilities. Second, its section on businesses says they should, through training, spread understanding of the Act, the Basic Policy and their sector guideline, and deepen understanding of disability so staff can respond appropriately. Third, it requires every sector guideline issued under Article 11 to address training and awareness, consultation systems, and internal rules or manuals.

The Basic Policy links training directly to accommodation with an example. A store trains its staff in advance on how to write on a customer's behalf on an application form (environmental improvement), and when a customer asks for that help, staff write for them while checking the customer's wishes (reasonable accommodation). The training is what makes the individual accommodation reliable.

The Basic Policy also asks training to cover points that are easy to miss: that women with disabilities and people with disabilities who are sexual minorities may face compounded barriers, and that children with disabilities have support needs different from adults.

sections.heading: What happens if a business does not comply?

blocks.text: There is no criminal penalty for failing to provide reasonable accommodation. Under Article 12, the competent minister may, where particularly necessary, require a report from the business or give advice, guidance or a recommendation based on the sector guideline.

Article 26 imposes a non-penal administrative fine of up to 200,000 yen on a business that fails to submit a report requested under Article 12 or submits a false one. The Basic Policy describes Article 12 action as a backstop for cases where a business repeatedly acts contrary to the Act and voluntary improvement cannot be expected.

sections.heading: How does this Act relate to accommodation for employees?

blocks.text: It does not cover a business's own workforce. Article 13 provides that measures a business takes as an employer toward its workers are governed by the Act on Promotion of Employment of Persons with Disabilities, which has its own accommodation provisions and guidance.

In practice, a training program needs two strands: one for staff who serve customers and the public under this Act, and one for managers and HR who handle employee accommodation under the employment statute. Mixing them tends to confuse the different legal tests and decision makers.

sections.heading: What should reasonable accommodation training cover?

items: The two Article 8 duties and the social model of disability, using the Basic Policy's definitions.
How to recognize an expression of need, including when it comes from a family member, assistant or interpreter on the person's behalf.
Constructive dialogue: asking what the person needs, what they usually do, and what alternatives exist.
The five excessive burden factors, who in the business may decide, and how to explain a refusal.
Sector specific examples from the competent ministry's guideline for your industry.
How to record requests and outcomes so the business can show what it did if asked under Article 12.

blocks.text: For structuring role based modules, see [role based training](/glossary/role-based-training) and [how to make elearning accessible](/guides/how-to-make-elearning-accessible), since training materials should themselves be accessible. Refresh cycles can follow [how to set mandatory training refresh cycles](/guides/how-to-set-mandatory-training-refresh-cycles).

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry models Article 8, Article 5 and the relevant sector guideline as linked obligations, with separate learning outcomes for front line staff, approving managers and desk staff. Each outcome carries an assessment point, such as a scenario on applying the five burden factors, so evidence of understanding sits alongside completion records.

faqs.q: Does reasonable accommodation apply if the person does not ask?
faqs.a: The legal duty in Article 8(2) is triggered by an expression of need, which can come from the person or from someone assisting them. The Basic Policy adds that where a need is obvious but the person cannot express it, the business should, in line with the Act's purpose, offer to discuss suitable accommodation.

faqs.q: Are online services covered by Japan's reasonable accommodation duty?
faqs.a: Yes. The Act covers business operators generally, and nothing limits it to physical premises. The Basic Policy treats information accessibility as part of environmental improvement. A request about an app, website or online form should be handled through the same dialogue and burden assessment.

faqs.q: Which ministry's guideline applies to my business?
faqs.a: Each competent minister issues a sector guideline under Article 11 for the businesses it oversees, such as financial services or healthcare. The Cabinet Office publishes a list of the ministries' guidelines and their consultation contacts. A business in several sectors should follow each relevant guideline.

faqs.q: Is staff training legally mandatory under the Act?
faqs.a: Article 5 sets an effort duty for staff training rather than a strict mandate, and there is no fixed curriculum or hours. In practice, a business that cannot show staff were trained will find it harder to show it handled requests properly if a ministry asks for a report under Article 12.
